titleText.es: Es todavía más difícil si eres el típico capullo que pronuncia los caracteres <>.
titleText.en: It's even harder if you're an asshole who pronounces <> brackets.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive closely translates the official title text. It calls the angle-bracket characters caracteres, while the official English wording calls them brackets; the joke depends on how code symbols are pronounced when counting a haiku's rhythm.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Here señales means clues or indications that suggest something is true, not road signs or posted notices.

example.es: Hay señales de que todo mejora.
example.en: There are signs that everything is improving.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; links señales to the evidence that follows
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Spanish uses de before que after señal or señales when the following clause states what the sign indicates. English normally expresses the combination as ‘a sign that...’ without a separate word for de.

example.es: Es una señal de que funciona.
example.en: It is a sign that it works.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: to; links a noun to an action available or needing to be done
cardDefinitions.noteEn: After a noun such as trabajo, algo, or nada, que can introduce an action in its unchanged dictionary form. Natural English often uses ‘to’ instead.

example.en: We have several tasks to finish.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Casi goes before the word or action that comes close to being true but is not fully complete.
Recuperado is the completed-action form of recuperar. With haber it says that a previous ability, level, or possession has been regained.

example.en: I have regained my previous pace.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Before a noun, antiguo or antigua can mean the earlier or former version of something rather than something ancient.

example.en: She returned to her former routine.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Escritura usually means writing. In a computing context, velocidad de escritura is the speed at which someone types.

example.es: Su escritura es más rápida con este teclado.
example.en: Her typing is faster with this keyboard.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: using; in (a keyboard layout or system)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: With the name of a keyboard layout, en identifies the system being used. Natural English often says ‘using’ that layout.
Nuestro changes to nuestros before more than one masculine or mixed-gender thing. The ending matches what is owned, not the people who own it.
In computing, a servidor is a computer or program that provides data or services to other computers.

example.es: Los servidores alojan la página web.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: they support; they are compatible with
cardDefinitions.noteEn: In a technical context, soportar means that a system can work with a protocol, format, or feature. It is not the physical sense of holding something up.
Cumplen is a plural form of cumplir. With con, it says that several things meet a rule, requirement, or standard.

example.es: Las páginas cumplen con la norma.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word here; links cumplir to a requirement or standard
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Cumplir con introduces the rule, promise, requirement, or standard that is met. English often uses ‘meet’ directly with no word for con.

example.es: El producto cumple con los requisitos.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: haiku; a short Japanese poetic form
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Haiku is used in Spanish for the Japanese poetic form. Here it names the poem type, not the Haiku operating system.

example.es: Escribió un haiku sobre la lluvia.
example.en: She wrote a haiku about the rain.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: webcomic; comic published on the web
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Webcómic combines web with cómic. Standard Spanish spelling keeps the written accent because the stressed syllable remains có.

example.en: She reads a webcomic every week.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How can a noun name something available, pending, or necessary to do?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Put que after the noun, then use the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The plus signs mean ‘followed by,’ sustantivo means a noun, and infinitivo means the unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form. Common examples include trabajo que hacer, algo que leer, and nada que decir.

example.en: There is a report to finish.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that something meets a requirement or standard?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use the matching form of cumplir, then con, then name the requirement or standard.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The plus sign means ‘followed by.’ Cumplir changes to match its subject, while con stays unchanged: cumple con for one thing and cumplen con for several things.

example.es: El diseño cumple con la norma.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: A haiku is a Japanese poetic form commonly taught outside Japan as three short lines following a 5–7–5 rhythm; the comic jokes that HTML markup can satisfy both code rules and poetic form.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The title text adds that the count becomes harder when angle brackets are pronounced aloud, making the way code symbols are read part of the joke.

applications.explanationEn: Oye is the irregular positive tú command of oír and is used here to get one familiar person's attention.
Habéis is the informal-plural helper used mainly in Spain, and visto is the completed-action form that follows it.
Habéis is the present-perfect helper for vosotros or vosotras, addressing several familiar people in the form common in Spain.
